s: Which of the following protected-cultivation practices grows crops in a controlled environment and can provide protection from weather, pests and diseases?
x: Protected cultivation in greenhouses, polytunnels or shade nets provides a controlled environment and protection from adverse weather, pests and diseases.

s: A farmer wants year-round crop production in a non-tropical or harsh setting by using stacked layers indoors under controlled conditions. Which technology is most appropriate?
x: Vertical farming grows crops in stacked indoor layers under controlled conditions and can provide year-round output even in non-tropical or harsh settings.

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Vertical farming — crops are grown only in open fields
Hydroponics — roots hang in air and are misted
Aeroponics — roots grow in nutrient-rich water
Aquaponics — fish culture is combined with hydroponics and fish waste feeds plants
x: Aquaponics combines fish culture with hydroponics, with fish waste supplying nutrients to plants. Hydroponics uses nutrient-rich water, while aeroponics suspends roots in air and mists them.

s: How are plant roots kept in aeroponics?
x: Aeroponics misted roots in air; hydroponics uses nutrient water and aquaponics fish waste.

s: Aquaponics combines hydroponics with which of the following?
x: Aquaponics combines fish culture with hydroponics; fish waste feeds plants.

s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly described?
o: Hydroponics – roots suspended in air and misted
x: Hydroponics grows roots in nutrient-rich water; misted roots in air is aeroponics.

s: What does direct-seeded rice involve, unlike transplanted rice?
x: Direct-seeded rice is planted without nursery raising or transplanting. It has also been promoted together with zero-till wheat under NICRA.

s: Alternate wetting and drying in the System of Rice Intensification mainly reduces the emission of which gas from paddy fields?
x: Alternate wetting and drying avoids continuous flooding, cutting methane production from paddies; SRI also uses less seed and saves electricity on pumping.

s: Which one of the following is NOT a stated feature of zero tillage?
o: Wheat can be sown without burning the previous crop residue.
It can contribute to soil carbon sequestration.
It necessarily requires complete removal of all crop residue before sowing.
Paddy seed can be planted directly without raising a nursery.
x: Zero tillage is associated with sowing wheat without burning previous residue, direct planting of paddy without a nursery, and soil carbon sequestration. Complete removal of residue is not a stated feature.

s: Which of the following practices helps conserve water in agriculture?
o: Repeated deep ploughing after every irrigation
Reduced or zero tillage with crop residue left on the field
x: Reduced or zero tillage combined with leaving crop residue helps conserve water. Gypsum application before irrigation is not identified as the water-conserving practice in this comparison.

s: How does laser land levelling save water?
o: Injecting air below the water table
Making the field surface uniform so water spreads evenly
x: Laser levelling gives a uniform surface so water spreads evenly.

s: What planting material does the Sustainable Sugarcane Initiative use?
x: SSI uses single-bud chips instead of setts, cutting seed cost, with wider spacing and drip.

s: Under which programme is direct-seeded rice promoted along with zero-till wheat?
x: Direct-seeded rice is promoted with zero-till wheat under NICRA.

s: Which irrigation method has the highest water-use efficiency, about 90%?
x: Drip irrigation is about 90% efficient, sprinklers about 70–80% and flood or furrow irrigation about 30–50%.

s: How does drip irrigation apply water?
o: Directly to the root zone through emitters
x: Drip delivers water to the root zone through emitters on lateral pipes; sprinklers spray pressurised water through nozzles like rainfall.

s: The shift in agricultural policy from ‘more output’ to ‘more output at lower ecological cost’ is associated with which concept?
x: The policy emphasis on higher output with lower ecological cost is described as the Evergreen Revolution, associated with M.S. Swaminathan.

s: Why does sprinkler irrigation lose more water to wind and evaporation than drip irrigation?
o: It uses emitters at the root zone
Its water travels through the air
x: Sprinklers spray water through the air, exposing it to wind and evaporation, while drip applies water at the roots.

s: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of fertigation?
o: Control of the alkalinity of irrigation water
Increased availability of nutrients to plants
Reduction in the leaching of chemical nutrients
x: Fertigation helps control water alkalinity, raises nutrient availability and reduces leaching; efficient application of rock phosphate is not one of its advantages.

s: What does fertigation refer to?
x: Fertigation is fertiliser applied through irrigation water, e.g. the drip line; efficient rock phosphate use is not one of its advantages.

s: What is the water-use efficiency of sprinkler irrigation?
x: Sprinkler efficiency is 70-80%, drip about 90% and flood 30-50%.

s: Who is associated with 'more output at lower ecological cost' (the Evergreen Revolution)?
x: The Evergreen Revolution idea is M.S. Swaminathan's.

s: What is the main limitation of drip irrigation?
o: It cannot be used for fertigation
x: Drip is the most efficient method (about 90%), but its main limit is the higher initial cost.

s: From 2022–23, Per Drop More Crop (PDMC) has been implemented under which scheme?
x: PDMC, launched in 2015–16, was part of PMKSY up to 2021–22 and has been implemented under RKVY since 2022–23.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Micro Irrigation Fund (MIF)?
o: It is a Rs 10,000 crore corpus with NABARD
Another Rs 5,000 crore was added for the 15th Finance Commission period
It was set up with an initial Rs 5,000 crore
It was operationalised in 2015-16 along with Per Drop More Crop
x: MIF was operationalised in 2019-20; it is Per Drop More Crop that began in 2015-16.

s: What type of scheme is PMKSY, with the State Agriculture Department as nodal authority?
x: PMKSY is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme and the State Agriculture Department is its nodal authority.

s: Under which scheme is the Andhra Pradesh Micro Irrigation Project implemented throughout the State with financial assistance?
x: The Andhra Pradesh Micro Irrigation Project is implemented State-wide under the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchai Yojana with financial assistance.

s: The gross irrigated area as a percentage of gross cropped area rose from about 41.7% in 2001-02 to what level?
x: The gross irrigated area increased from 41.7% in 2001-02 to 55.8% in 2022-23.

s: Which areas receive priority under Per Drop More Crop?
o: Rainfed areas, water-stressed districts and critical groundwater blocks
Only command areas with assured canal irrigation
x: The priority areas are rainfed regions, water-stressed districts and critical groundwater blocks.

s: With which institution is the Micro Irrigation Fund corpus maintained?
x: The Rs 10,000 crore Micro Irrigation Fund is with NABARD, not RBI.

s: In which year was Per Drop More Crop launched?
x: PDMC was launched in 2015-16; it moved to RKVY from 2022-23.

s: What is the subsidy for micro-irrigation under NMSA (PM-RKVY)?
x: NMSA gives up to 55% subsidy for micro-irrigation, capped at 5 ha.

s:
Consider the following statements about Per Drop More Crop:
1. It is implemented under RKVY from 2022-23.
2. Rainfed areas and critical groundwater blocks get priority.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both are correct: PDMC moved from PMKSY to RKVY in 2022-23 and prioritises rainfed areas and critical groundwater blocks.

s: About how much area was brought under micro-irrigation through Per Drop More Crop from 2015-16 to 2025-26?
x: About 102 lakh ha came under micro-irrigation through PDMC in this period.

s: About how many Soil Health Cards had been issued in India by November 2025?
x: About 25.55 crore Soil Health Cards had been issued by November 2025.

s: The AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 identifies which of the following as key areas of focus?
x: APSES 2024-25 records large-scale drip and sprinkler irrigation and names precision farming, drones and IoT as focus areas.

s: Which State ranked first in India in micro-irrigation implementation in 2024–25?
x: Andhra Pradesh ranked first in India in micro-irrigation implementation in 2024–25.

s: Under APMIP, SC/ST small and marginal farmers get what subsidy for drip irrigation?
x: SC/ST small and marginal farmers get 100% (cap Rs 2 lakh); other small and marginal 90%.

s: Which district leads Andhra Pradesh in micro-irrigation implementation?
x: AP ranked 1st in India in 2024-25, led by Ananthapuramu.

s: Under APMIP, farmers with 5-10 acres get what drip subsidy?
x: Farmers with 5-10 acres get 70%; above 10 acres 50%.

s: Where is the automation-based micro-irrigation facility launched in January 2026?
x: It is at the Integrated Water Resources Management and Farmer Training Centre, Governorpet, Vijayawada.

s: Which Andhra Pradesh Agriculture Minister launched automation-based micro-irrigation at Governorpet, Vijayawada, in January 2026?
x: On 7 January 2026 Agriculture Minister K. Atchannaidu launched sensor-based automated micro-irrigation at Governorpet, Vijayawada.

s: GPS, drones, artificial intelligence and sensors are identified as core elements of which agricultural approach?
o: The Second Green Revolution and sustainable intensification
x: GPS, drones, AI and sensors form the technological core of the Second Green Revolution and sustainable intensification.

s: What does variable-rate technology in agriculture refer to?
o: changing the crop variety every season without field data
applying the same quantity of inputs throughout a field
using only variable rainfall for crop production
applying inputs at varying rates within a field according to sensor or GIS maps
x: Variable-rate technology applies agricultural inputs at different rates within a field, based on sensor information or GIS maps.

s: Which centre, set up in 2012, runs ISRO's crop forecasting under FASAL?
x: The Mahalanobis National Crop Forecast Centre (2012) runs ISRO's FASAL crop forecasting.

s: Under which scheme does the KISAN project (October 2015) use space technology for crop cutting experiments?
x: KISAN uses space technology for Crop Cutting Experiments under PMFBY.

s: Which body maps soils from satellite data using GIS?
o: Soil and Land Use Survey of India
x: The Soil and Land Use Survey of India maps soils from satellite data; MNCFC runs FASAL.

s: Through which of the following does Drone Shakti build the drone ecosystem?
o: manufacturing and Remote Pilot Certificate training
x: Drone Shakti supports the drone ecosystem through manufacturing and training for Remote Pilot Certificates.

s: Which of the following correctly describes the Drone Corporation of Andhra Pradesh?
o: A privately owned body providing only drone imports
A central regulatory authority under the Ministry of Civil Aviation
x: The Drone Corporation of Andhra Pradesh is State-owned and provides drone-as-a-service.

s: For which of the following are Kisan drones used?
o: Eliminating the need for irrigation water
Crop assessment, soil health analysis and spraying
x: Kisan drones assess crops, analyse soil health and spray inputs, reducing human exposure to chemicals; they do not remove the need for irrigation.

s: Which authority regulates agricultural drones under the Drone Rules, 2021?
o: Soil and Land Use Survey of India
x: Agricultural drones are regulated by the Directorate General of Civil Aviation under the Drone Rules, 2021.

s: To whom does the Namo Drone Didi scheme provide drones?
x: Namo Drone Didi gives drones to women SHGs, who rent them out for spraying.

s:
Consider the following statements about Namo Drone Didi:
1. Its target is 15,000 drones.
2. Its outlay is Rs 1,261 crore.
3. Central assistance is 50% of the drone cost.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The target is 15,000 drones with an outlay of Rs 1,261 crore; central assistance is 80% (max Rs 8 lakh), not 50%.

s: Who released the Standard Operating Procedures for using drones to spray pesticides and soil and crop nutrients in December 2021?
x: Union Agriculture Minister Narendra Singh Tomar released the drone-spraying SOPs on 21 December 2021.

s: What is AgriStack?
o: an Aadhaar-like digital public good built through a federated Centre-State approach
a satellite used for crop forecasting
a centralised crop insurance claim portal managed only by States
x: AgriStack is described as an Aadhaar-like digital public good developed through a federated Centre-State build.

s: Which of the following pairs relating to the Digital Agriculture Mission is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Digital public infrastructure – Soil Fertility Profile
x: The mission's outlay is Rs 2,817 crore, not Rs 28,170 crore; it was approved in September 2024 and its DPI includes AgriStack, Krishi DSS and the Soil Fertility Profile.

s: Krishi Decision Support System integrates which combination of data?
o: Satellite, weather, soil and crop data
Only farmer identity and bank-account data
x: Krishi DSS joins satellite, weather, soil and crop data.

s: Through which centres does AP e-Crop booking (e-Panta) register crops digitally?
x: e-Panta registers crops through Rythu Bharosa Kendras; it is the base record for welfare and crop-loss relief.

s: What does the digital crop survey under the Digital Agriculture Mission record?
x: The digital crop survey gives plot-level, real-time crop acreage.

s: What is the outlay of the Digital Agriculture Mission (September 2024)?
x: The Digital Agriculture Mission outlay is Rs 2,817 crore.

s: Which State created the FRUITS unified farmer database in 2020?
x: Karnataka built FRUITS (2020), a unified farmer database.

s: What does Component A of PM-KUSUM relate to?
o: Installation of standalone off-grid solar pumps
Solarisation of existing grid-connected agricultural pumps
Decentralised grid-connected solar/renewable power plants on barren or fallow land
x: Component A of PM-KUSUM covers decentralised grid-connected solar/renewable plants on barren or fallow land. Standalone pumps and solarisation of grid-connected pumps are the other components.

s: Kisan e-Mitra is an AI chatbot that answers queries related to which of the following?
x: Kisan e-Mitra uses AI to answer PM-KISAN queries in several languages.

s: What does Component B of PM-KUSUM relate to?
o: Grid-connected solar plants on barren land
x: B covers standalone solar pumps; A is grid-connected plants on barren land and C solarising grid-connected pumps.

s: PM-KUSUM (2019) is run by which ministry?
x: PM-KUSUM is an MNRE scheme launched in 2019.

s: Which component of PM-KUSUM relates to solarising existing grid-connected agricultural pumps?
x: Component C solarises grid-connected pumps; A is solar plants on barren land and B is standalone solar pumps.

s: What is copying or amplifying a desired gene or DNA fragment called?
x: Gene cloning copies a desired gene; whole-animal cloning copies a complete organism.

s: In biotechnology, what is a collection of genetic material called?
x: A genetic library is a collection of genetic material; gene cloning copies a gene and biochips aid drug discovery.

s: Microbial production of useful products is an application of biotechnology in which field?
x: In industry biotechnology gives microbial products; in agriculture GM crops, in medicine drugs and vaccines, and in research biochips.

s: In the classic GMO application, the human insulin gene is put into which of the following to produce insulin?
x: The human insulin gene is put into bacteria, which then make insulin.

s: In producing a GMO, genetic engineering transfers genes in ways that:
x: Genetic engineering changes the genome by moving genes, often from another organism, in ways that would not happen naturally.

s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: GMO – Broad term for any organism whose genome is altered by genetic engineering
Transgenic crops – Biotechnology or agricultural application
Transgenic organism – Carries a foreign gene from another species
Purpose of a transgenic organism – Organism carrying a foreign gene from another species
x: The purpose of a transgenic organism is a desired characteristic or product; carrying a foreign gene from another species is what defines the transgenic organism itself.

s:
Arrange the following steps of recombinant DNA technology in the correct sequence:
A. Formation of recombinant DNA by joining fragments with DNA ligase
B. Isolation of DNA
C. Insertion into a host cell
D. Cutting DNA at specific sites by restriction endonucleases
x: DNA is first isolated, then cut at specific sites, joined by DNA ligase to form recombinant DNA, and finally inserted into a host cell.

s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: A restriction enzyme is also called a restriction endonuclease.
A restriction enzyme cuts DNA at or near specific recognition sites.
A restriction enzyme cuts DNA only at random locations.
A restriction enzyme cleaves DNA into fragments.
x: Option C is incorrect: restriction enzymes cut at specific recognition sequences, not at random. They are also called restriction endonucleases.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: pBR322 – Early widely used E. coli cloning vector
x: pBR322 was an early, widely used E. coli cloning vector; DNA ligase is the molecular stitcher and PCR amplifies DNA.

s: What is PCR (polymerase chain reaction) a technique for?
o: Copying small quantities of DNA for analysis
x: PCR copies small amounts of DNA for molecular analysis, diagnostic testing and research.

s: Why is Agrobacterium tumefaciens commonly used in plant genetic engineering?
o: Its ribosomes replace the plant cell nucleus.
Its disarmed Ti plasmid transfers T-DNA into the plant nucleus.
It destroys all plant viruses without transferring DNA.
It produces human insulin directly in plant leaves.
x: Agrobacterium tumefaciens is called nature's genetic engineer because T-DNA from its disarmed Ti plasmid can carry the desired gene into the plant nucleus.

s: By which process is a recombinant plasmid introduced into a bacterium?
x: The recombinant plasmid enters the bacterium by transformation, and rapid bacterial multiplication then yields large quantities of DNA or product.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about plasmids?
o: Plasmids are usually linear, single-stranded DNA
Some natural plasmid genes confer antibiotic resistance
Experimental plasmids are used as vectors
Plasmids are used to clone, transfer and manipulate genes
x: Plasmids are usually circular, double-stranded DNA, not linear single-stranded DNA.

s: In recombinant DNA technology, which enzyme joins DNA fragments?
x: DNA ligase joins the fragments; restriction endonucleases cut DNA.

s: What do the letters 'BR' stand for in the plasmid vector pBR322?
x: pBR322 is an early E. coli vector: p = plasmid, BR = Bolivar and Rodriguez.

s: Which organism is called 'Nature's genetic engineer'?
x: Agrobacterium tumefaciens is nature's genetic engineer; its disarmed Ti plasmid carries T-DNA into plants.

s: Which technique is used for gene silencing?
x: RNA interference (RNAi) silences genes; PCR amplifies DNA.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: Bt cotton was approved in India in 2002. Humulin came in 1982, Flavr Savr in 1994 and CRISPR-Cas9 was shown in 2012.

s: Which condition in the gut of the insect larva activates the inactive Bt protoxin?
x: The protoxin is activated in the alkaline gut of the larva; the active toxin then binds midgut cells and creates pores.

s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes Bollgard I from Bollgard II?
o: Bollgard I is herbicide-tolerant, whereas Bollgard II is drought-tolerant.
Bollgard I contains Cry1Ac, whereas Bollgard II contains Cry1Ac and Cry2Ab.
Bollgard I contains Cry2Ab, whereas Bollgard II contains only Cry1Ac.
Both contain only Cry2Ab but differ in the host plant.
x: Bollgard I, introduced in 2002, contains Cry1Ac. Bollgard II, introduced in 2006, combines Cry1Ac and Cry2Ab.

s: In which year was Bt cotton approved for commercial cultivation in India?
x: Bt cotton was approved in March 2002 (three MAHYCO hybrids); 2006 is when Bollgard II came.

s: By about how much has Bt cotton, which covers about 90% of India's cotton area, cut pesticide use?
x: The cut in pesticide use is about 40-50%, not 70-80%; Bt cotton covers about 90% of the cotton area (~10.8 million ha).

s: Which pest has developed resistance to the Bt toxins of Bt cotton?
x: The pink bollworm has overcome Bt toxins; whitefly and mealybug are sucking pests whose numbers rose, a separate problem.

s: Bt cotton is claimed to reduce pesticide use mainly because the plant:
o: Produces its own insecticidal Bt toxin
x: Bt cotton carries a Bacillus thuringiensis gene and makes its own insecticidal toxin, so less pesticide is sprayed.

s: Experiments on Bt proteins in agricultural soil have shown that they:
o: Can be removed only by burning crop residue
x: Although persistence of Bt proteins in soil was feared, experiments have shown that they degrade.

s: In which year was the second-generation Bt cotton, Bollgard II, introduced?
x: Bollgard I came in 2002 and Bollgard II, with Cry1Ac + Cry2Ab, in 2006.

s: Which sucking pests have risen as a problem in Bt cotton fields?
x: Bt cotton has seen a rise of sucking pests such as whitefly and mealybug, besides pink bollworm resistance.

s: Which State is the largest producer of Bt cotton in India?
x: Maharashtra is India's largest Bt cotton producer.

s: The Bt cotton hybrids approved in India in March 2002 were mainly meant to control which pest?
x: The three MAHYCO Bt cotton hybrids of 2002 targeted the American bollworm.

s: Whose three hybrids were the first Bt cotton approved in India in March 2002?
x: In March 2002 three MAHYCO Bt cotton hybrids were approved against the American bollworm.

s: HTBt cotton combines the Bt trait with tolerance to which herbicide?
x: HTBt cotton combines the Bt trait with tolerance to the herbicide glyphosate. It is not approved in India, so growing it is illegal.

s: A 2025-26 study found illegal HTBt cotton on about what share of the cotton area in Andhra Pradesh?
x: Illegal HTBt cotton covered about 15-18% of cotton area in AP and 27-30% in Telangana.

s:
Consider the following statements about HTBt cotton:
1. It combines the Bt trait with glyphosate tolerance.
2. It is approved for commercial cultivation in India.
3. Labour shortage and cheap glyphosate weeding drive its spread.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: HTBt cotton adds glyphosate tolerance to Bt and spreads because of labour shortage and cheap weeding, but it is not approved and is illegal.

s: To curb illegal HTBt cotton, the use of which herbicide was restricted in Andhra Pradesh?
x: Illegal HTBt cotton tolerates glyphosate, so Andhra Pradesh restricted glyphosate use.

s: Which State is recognised as the leading Bt cotton-growing State in India?
x: Maharashtra is identified as the leading Bt cotton State.

s: Through which of the following does biofortification usually raise the nutrient level of crops?
x: Biofortification generally raises nutritional value through conventional breeding, whereas GM technology inserts foreign genes.

s: Which company dropped its Roundup Ready GM wheat on 10 May 2004, citing market resistance?
x: Monsanto announced on 10 May 2004 that it would not introduce Roundup Ready wheat.

s: Who developed Golden Rice?
x: Golden Rice was developed by Ingo Potrykus and Peter Beyer.

s: Golden Rice was developed to fight the deficiency of which vitamin?
x: Golden Rice makes beta-carotene, which the body turns into vitamin A.

s: Golden Rice is designed to enhance the biosynthesis of which substance?
o: Beta-carotene, a precursor of Vitamin A
x: Golden Rice is designed for beta-carotene biosynthesis, linked to Vitamin A nutrition.

s: In which year was human insulin first marketed as Humulin?
x: Humulin was marketed in 1982, after the first GMO in 1973; CRISPR-Cas9 was demonstrated in 2012.

s: The Flavr Savr tomato, developed by Calgene in the United States in 1994, was notable because it was the first commercially sold GM food and had which characteristic?
o: Resistance to the fruit and shoot borer
Delayed ripening and a longer shelf life
x: Flavr Savr was the first commercially sold genetically modified food. Its delayed ripening provided a longer shelf life.

s: In which year was the first GMO produced?
x: The first GMO dates to 1973; 1982 is Humulin, 1994 Flavr Savr and 2002 Bt cotton approval in India.

s: Which company made Humulin, the first human hormone produced by recombinant DNA technology (1982)?
x: Humulin (human insulin) was made by Eli Lilly in 1982; Calgene made the Flavr Savr tomato.

s: Mon 863, in the news over the safety of feeding studies, was which genetically modified crop?
o: Vitamin-A enriched rice targeting night blindness
x: Mon 863 was a Monsanto genetically modified pest-resistant maize variety directed against corn rootworm and was discussed in connection with feeding-study safety.

s: Which of the following did the Flavr Savr tomato use to achieve delayed ripening?
x: Flavr Savr used antisense polygalacturonase for delayed ripening.

s: What is the full form of CRISPR?
o: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Small Palindromic Repeats
Clustered Repeatedly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats
Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats
Clustered Regularly Integrated Short Palindromic Repeats
x: CRISPR stands for Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats. The other options change one word.

s: In CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing, which component guides Cas9 to the desired genomic location?
x: Guide RNA leads the Cas9 enzyme to the target site; CRISPR itself is specialised stretches of DNA.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about CRISPR-Cas9?
o: It can be used to correct genetic defects
It can be used to improve crops
Its guide RNA acts as the molecular scissors
x: Cas9 is the molecular scissors and the guide RNA is the navigator; CRISPR can fix genetic defects and improve crops, and it raises ethical concerns.

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with Pusa Rice DST1?
o: Edited version of MTU1010 — rice bred at Maruteru in Andhra Pradesh
Transgenic version of AquAdvantage — salmon bred in Punjab
Bt version of IR8 — rice bred in Colombia
Gene-drive version of MTU1010 — mosquito bred in Maruteru
x: Pusa Rice DST1 is an edited version of MTU1010, an Andhra Pradesh-bred rice variety associated with Maruteru.

s: To which stresses is the genome-edited Pusa Rice DST1 tolerant?
x: Pusa Rice DST1 is genome-edited for drought and salinity tolerance, giving about 10-30% higher yield under stress without foreign DNA.

s: Which site-directed nuclease category uses a template but introduces no foreign DNA?
x: SDN-2 uses a template but adds no foreign DNA and is exempt under the 2022 guidelines; SDN-1 uses no template and SDN-3 inserts foreign DNA.

s: Base editing differs from conventional double-strand-break editing because it:
o: Changes proteins without altering DNA bases
Converts one DNA base into another without creating double-strand breaks
Works exclusively by destroying the host cell
x: Base editing converts one DNA base into another without producing double-strand breaks in the DNA.

s: Where is the Centre of Excellence for CRISPR Innovation and Translation (CoE-CIT) to be set up?
x: The CoE-CIT is to be set up in Bengaluru.

s: Who received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for CRISPR-Cas9?
x: Doudna and Charpentier showed CRISPR-Cas9 in 2012 and won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020.

s: What is ICAR's indigenous, smaller alternative to Cas9 for genome editing?
x: TnpB, developed by ICAR, is an indigenous and smaller alternative to Cas9.

s: Which institute developed the genome-edited rice DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala)?
x: Kamala (DRR Dhan 100) comes from ICAR-IIRR, Hyderabad, from Samba Mahsuri; Pusa DST Rice 1 is from ICAR-IARI.

s: In which year were India's first genome-edited rice varieties released?
x: India became the first to release genome-edited rice on 4 May 2025; 2022 is the year SDN-1/2 were exempted.

s: In the CRISPR-Cas9 system, which component acts as the molecular scissors?
x: Cas9 cuts the DNA and is the molecular scissors; the guide RNA only acts as the navigator.

s: Pusa DST Rice 1 was made by editing which variety bred at Maruteru, Andhra Pradesh?
x: Pusa DST Rice 1 is edited MTU1010, a variety bred at Maruteru, AP; Kamala is from Samba Mahsuri.

s: CRISPR, now used for genome editing, is originally a natural defence system of which organisms?
x: CRISPR is a natural defence system of bacteria and archaea against viruses.

s: Concern over which of the following stopped the commercial release of a soybean variety containing a Brazil-nut gene?
x: The Brazil-nut gene was intended to improve methionine content, but the resulting soybean raised allergy concerns and was therefore never released.

s: What does horizontal gene transfer refer to in the biosafety context?
o: Replacement of nuclear DNA by mitochondrial DNA in every cell
Movement of genes between unrelated organisms
Transmission of genes only from parent to offspring
Movement of pollen only within one flower
x: Horizontal gene transfer is the movement of genes between unrelated organisms. Antibiotic-resistance genes may potentially pass from environmental bacteria to human pathogens.

s: Which one of the following is regarded as the primary environmental concern about the cultivation of GM crops?
o: Transgenes moving by cross-pollination into non-GM crops and wild relatives
x: Gene flow, the movement of transgenes by pollen into non-GM crops and wild relatives, is the primary environmental concern (PYQ). It can create superweeds and alter native gene pools. The other options are not GM-crop concerns.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the risks of Bt toxins and other engineered traits?
o: They may affect pollinators and natural enemies of pests
They may affect soil nematodes and microbes
Lasting persistence of Bt proteins in soil is the proven main GM risk
x: Bt proteins degrade in soil and lasting persistence is not proven; gene flow is the main GM risk. Non-target harm to pollinators, soil life and aquatic organisms is a real concern.

s: V-GURT (terminator technology) is banned in India under which Act?
x: V-GURT, which makes plants produce sterile seeds, is banned in India under the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001.

s: A key gene-flow argument against Bt brinjal was that India is a centre of diversity of which crop?
x: Transgene escape risk is highest in a crop's centre of diversity, and India is a centre of diversity of brinjal itself.

s: Which one of the following best explains genetic homogenisation in agriculture?
o: Cultivation of many locally adapted landraces in small farms
Increase in the number of unrelated crop species in a field
Exchange of seeds among farmers without commercial restrictions
Use of uniform engineered varieties over large areas, reducing agro-biodiversity
x: Genetic homogenisation results when uniform varieties are widely cultivated, reducing agro-biodiversity and increasing vulnerability to new pathogens and climate shocks.

s: What can movement of transgenes through pollen into wild relatives give rise to?
x: Gene flow by pollen into non-GM crops and wild relatives can create superweeds and alter gene pools.

s: What fear do antibiotic-resistance marker genes in GM crops raise?
x: Antibiotic-resistance markers raise fear that resistance may spread to pathogens.

s: Which GURT type switches a trait on or off by applying a chemical?
x: T-GURT (traitor) switches a trait by a chemical and is at research stage; V-GURT (terminator) gives sterile seeds.

s: Which fund under the PPV&FR Act, 2001 is meant for benefit sharing?
x: The PPV&FR Act sets up the National Gene Fund for benefit sharing.

s: Mitochondrial Replacement Therapy is popularly known as the ____ technique, and its main ethical concern relates to ____.
o: three-parent baby; germline editing and designer babies
three-parent baby; pollen sterility in crops
synthetic-embryo; germline editing and designer babies
x: MRT is the 'three-parent baby' technique and raises ethical issues of germline editing and designer babies (A). B has the wrong name and concern; C has the right name but a crop issue; D has the right concern but the wrong name.

s: In synthetic biology, in which organism has semaglutide been grown?
x: Semaglutide was grown in baker's yeast; Bacillus thuringiensis is the source of Bt genes.

s: What is the basic idea of gene therapy?
o: Change the environmental conditions of the patient
Alter, replace or correct defective genetic function
Replace damaged tissue with artificial implants
x: Gene therapy is a genetic-engineering application that alters, replaces or corrects defective genes; it does not change the environment.

s: Which field relates an individual's genetics to drug response?
x: Pharmacogenomics links genes to drug response and supports personalised or precision medicine.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about genetic medicine?
o: Gene therapy alters, replaces or corrects defective genes
Hepatitis B and HPV vaccines are recombinant vaccines
Mitochondrial replacement therapy is called the three-parent baby technique
x: Pharmacogenomics relates genes to drug response; gene silencing is RNAi.

s: In which year did CDSCO rules on gene therapy come into force in India?
x: Gene therapy alters or corrects defective genes, and CDSCO issued rules on it in 2023.

s: What role do engineered viruses and lipid nanoparticles play in genetic medicine?
o: Carriers to deliver the medicine into cells
Probes that detect pathogens in blood
Enzymes that cut DNA at specific sites
x: Genetic medicines, which correct or compensate for faulty genes, are delivered by engineered viruses and lipid nanoparticles.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about gene-drive mosquitoes?
o: Population suppression aims to make the mosquito unable to support parasite development
Over 90% of offspring inherit the drive instead of the normal 50%
A CRISPR-Cas9 gene drive copies itself onto the partner chromosome
'Transmission Zero' is a Tanzania-led project on GM mosquitoes
x: This reverses the two types: population suppression uses sterile females, while population modification stops the parasite developing.

s: AquAdvantage, whose escapees may out-compete wild stock, is a genetically modified form of which organism?
x: AquAdvantage is a GM salmon; escapees may out-compete wild fish.

s: With a gene drive, what share of GM mosquito offspring inherit the trait?
x: Gene drives make more than 90% of offspring inherit the trait, against the normal 50%.

s: Which of the following is a distinctive concern associated with gene-drive mosquitoes?
o: The released trait can be recalled easily by stopping pesticide application.
The trait may spread through wild populations and there is no simple recall mechanism.
The technology is incapable of affecting mosquito populations.
The trait remains confined to the laboratory by definition.
x: Gene drives may spread a trait through wild populations, potentially causing population collapse or producing malaria-resistant mosquitoes. Unlike pesticide use, there is no simple recall mechanism.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Bt brinjal?
o: The GEAC recommended its release in 2009
It was developed through collaboration among Mahyco, UAS Dharwad and TNAU
Its principal target was the fruit and shoot borer
The moratorium on it was imposed in 2012
x: The moratorium on Bt brinjal was imposed in 2010 by Jairam Ramesh, not 2012; the other statements are correct.

s: Who developed GM mustard DMH-11 (Dhara Mustard Hybrid-11)?
o: Delhi University (Centre for Genetic Manipulation of Crop Plants)
x: DMH-11 was developed at Delhi University's CGMCP (Deepak Pental). MAHYCO with UAS Dharwad and TNAU developed Bt brinjal; ICAR-IARI developed genome-edited Pusa Rice DST1.

s: Under which scientist was GM mustard DMH-11 developed at Delhi University's CGMCP?
x: DMH-11 was developed by Delhi University's CGMCP led by Deepak Pental.

s: In which year was Bt brinjal, recommended by GEAC in 2009, put under a moratorium?
x: GEAC recommended Bt brinjal in 2009 and Jairam Ramesh imposed a moratorium in 2010.

s: Against which of the following was Bt brinjal developed for resistance?
x: Bt brinjal was developed for resistance to the fruit and shoot borer insect.

s: From which bacterium do the barnase-barstar genes used in GM mustard DMH-11 come?
x: Barnase-barstar comes from Bacillus amyloliquefaciens; Bacillus thuringiensis is the source of Bt genes. DMH-11 was developed by Delhi University.

s: Which statement correctly describes Bollgard II cotton?
o: It uses the barnase-barstar system from Bacillus amyloliquefaciens
It contains only the antisense polygalacturonase gene
It contains Cry1Ac and Cry2Ab from Bacillus thuringiensis
It produces beta-carotene using daffodil genes alone
x: Bollgard II cotton contains Cry1Ac and Cry2Ab genes sourced from Bacillus thuringiensis. The other options describe Flavr Savr, Golden Rice or GM mustard.

s: Bt brinjal carries which gene against the fruit and shoot borer?
x: Bt brinjal uses the Cry1Ac gene against the fruit and shoot borer.

s: What kind of ruling did the Supreme Court give on GM mustard DMH-11 in July 2024?
o: Dismissal of the case as withdrawn
x: The July 2024 verdict was split, though both judges directed the Centre to frame a national GM crop policy; GEAC had cleared its environmental release in 2022.

s: What did the Supreme Court-appointed Technical Expert Committee of 2013 recommend?
o: A 10-year moratorium on GM field trials
x: The 2013 Technical Expert Committee recommended a 10-year moratorium on field trials.

s: In which year did GEAC clear the environmental release of GM mustard DMH-11?
x: GEAC cleared DMH-11 in 2017 but the Ministry withheld it; environmental release was cleared on 18 October 2022.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Farmers in Maharashtra and Haryana grew unapproved GM crops to protest against approval delays.
2. Bt cotton is the only GM crop commercially cultivated in India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Farmers in Maharashtra and Haryana defied the rules, and Bt cotton remains the only commercial GM crop.

s: Besides Bt cotton, which unapproved GM crop did farmers in Maharashtra and Haryana grow in defiance of the rules?
x: Farmers there grew unapproved Bt cotton and Bt brinjal to protest delays.

s: Who imposed the moratorium on Bt brinjal in 2010?
x: Environment Minister Jairam Ramesh imposed the Bt brinjal moratorium in 2010, after GEAC's 2009 recommendation.

s: Approval of a GM product in India may take about 7-10 years. About how long does it take globally?
x: Overlapping mandates of DBT, GEAC, CDSCO, FSSAI and NBA and the lack of a biosafety liability law mean 7–10 years in India against 3–5 years globally.

s: Through which gene does GM mustard DMH-11 also carry herbicide tolerance?
x: DMH-11 carries the bar gene, which gives herbicide tolerance and fuels public resistance.

s: In July 2024, which body directed the Centre to frame a national GM crop policy?
x: In its July 2024 split verdict on DMH-11, both Supreme Court judges directed the Centre to frame a national GM crop policy.

s: Who chairs the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee?
o: The Special or Additional Secretary of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
The Chairperson of the Central Pollution Control Board
The Director-General of the Indian Council of Agricultural Research
x: GEAC is chaired by a Special or Additional Secretary of MoEFCC. A senior officer from the Department of Biotechnology serves as co-chair.

s: Which of the following is a function of the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee?
o: Fixing the maximum retail price of commercial seeds
Taking punitive action at the State level
Field-level monitoring at the district level
Approving large-scale use of hazardous microorganisms and recombinants
x: GEAC clears field trials, environmental release, commercial cultivation and large-scale use of hazardous microorganisms and recombinants; seed MRP is not its job.

s: In which year was the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee renamed the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee?
x: GEAC, constituted under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, was renamed from 'Approval' to 'Appraisal' in 2010.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: NGT – Established under the NGT Act, 2010
GEAC – Established under the NGT Act, 2010
CGWA – Constituted under the Water Act, 1974
CPCB – Constituted under Section 3(3) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
x: The NGT was established under the NGT Act, 2010. CGWA was set up under Section 3(3) of the EPA, CPCB under the Water Act, 1974, and GEAC deals with genetically engineered organisms.

s: The 2010 decision relating to Bt brinjal included which of the following additional measures?
o: A requirement that all GM seeds be branded by the State
A transfer of field-trial approval exclusively to FSSAI
A mandatory State no-objection certificate for field trials
A permanent ban on every GM crop in India
x: In 2010, a State NOC was made mandatory for field trials. The decision was not a permanent ban on every GM crop or a transfer of approval to FSSAI.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Eco-Sensitive Zone – Activities regulated, not necessarily prohibited
x: Activities in Eco-Sensitive Zones are regulated rather than banned. NGT comes from the NGT Act 2010, CGWA from Section 3(3) of EPA and CPCB from the Water Act 1974.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. GEAC functions under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change.
2. GEAC works under the Rules, 1989 framed under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
3. RCGM, which advises GEAC, functions under the Department of Biotechnology.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: GEAC is under MoEFCC and the Rules, 1989 of the EPA; RCGM is under DBT and only advises GEAC.

s: From which department is the co-chair of the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee drawn?
x: GEAC is chaired by a Special/Additional Secretary of MoEFCC, with a co-chair from DBT.

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: SBCC — State-level inspection, investigation and punitive action
DLC — Approval of all commercial GM releases
x: SBCC operates at the state level and has powers to inspect, investigate and take punitive action. DLC performs district-level monitoring, GEAC deals with environmental release and commercial use, and IBSC is institutional.

s: Which body forms the first, institutional-level tier of India's biosafety system?
x: The sequence begins with IBSC at institutional level, followed by RCGM, GEAC, SBCC, DLC and expert committees.

s: Under the Rules, 1989, which body approves the environmental release and commercial use of GM crops?
x: GEAC under MoEFCC approves environmental release and commercial use; RCGM under DBT only monitors research and advises GEAC.

s: Under which category are field trials of GM crops conducted in India?
x: GM field trials are run as Biosafety Research Level trials, BRL-I and BRL-II.

s: Which of the following is NOT one of the competent authorities under the Rules, 1989?
x: The six competent authorities are RDAC, IBSC, RCGM, GEAC, SBCC and DLC; FSSAI is not one of them.

s: Since 2010, what has been mandatory for conducting GM crop field trials?
x: Since 2010 a State NOC is mandatory for field trials, and several States refuse it.

s: Which committee under the Rules, 1989 can inspect, investigate and take punitive action at the State level?
x: The SBCC acts at State level with powers to inspect, investigate and punish; DLC monitors at district level.

s: Which committee under the Rules, 1989 functions under the Department of Biotechnology, monitors ongoing GM research and advises GEAC?
x: RCGM is under DBT; it monitors research and advises GEAC but does not approve release.

s:
Arrange the following biosafety bodies under the Rules, 1989 in the order of the approval chain:
1. GEAC
2. IBSC
3. RCGM
4. SBCC
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: The sequence is IBSC (institution) -> RCGM (DBT) -> GEAC (MoEFCC) -> SBCC (State) -> DLC (district).

s: Which provision of the Patents Act excludes plants, animals, seeds and essentially biological processes from patentability while permitting patenting of microbial processes?
x: Section 3(j) excludes plants, animals, seeds and essentially biological processes from patentability, while microbial processes can be patented.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Section 3(d) of the Patents Act?
o: It bars a patent for a new form of a known substance unless it shows enhanced efficacy
It is meant to block evergreening
In Novartis v Union of India (2013), the Glivec rejection was upheld under Section 3(j), not 3(d)
Section 3(j), a different clause, excludes plants, animals and seeds
x: The Supreme Court upheld the Glivec (imatinib) rejection under Section 3(d); Section 3(j) deals with plants, animals, seeds and essentially biological processes.

s: Under the PPV&FR Act, 2001, which of the following are farmers NOT allowed to sell?
x: Farmers may save, use, sow, resow, exchange, share and sell farm produce including seed, but not branded seed of protected varieties.

s: In the FL-2027 (FC5) potato variety case, PepsiCo sued farmers of which State?
x: PepsiCo sued Gujarat farmers, later withdrew the suits, and the PPVFR Authority revoked the variety's registration in 2021.

s: Which of the following is an objection raised by farmers against GURT or terminator seeds?
x: Farmers object to dependence on companies, recurring seed costs and the loss of seed-saving.

s: Which one of the following statements about the PPVFR Act and GURT is correct?
o: The Act mandates registration of all varieties carrying GURT.
The Act bars registration of varieties carrying GURT.
The Act has no provision concerning GURT.
The Act permits registration only when farmers cannot save seed.
x: The PPVFR Act bars registration of varieties carrying Genetic Use Restriction Technology. This reflects concerns over seed dependency and loss of farmers' seed-saving rights.

s: In Novartis v Union of India (2013), the Supreme Court upheld the rejection of a patent on which of the following?
x: The SC upheld rejection of the Glivec (imatinib) patent under Section 3(d), which blocks evergreening.

s: Which body's challenge led to the revocation of the US patent on turmeric for wound healing?
x: The 1995 US turmeric patent was revoked after CSIR challenged it.

s: Where did India win the neem biopiracy case?
x: India won the neem (anti-fungal) case at the European Patent Office.

s: Which company held the 1997 US patent on basmati rice, challenged by CSIR?
x: RiceTec of the USA held the 1997 basmati patent; key claims were disallowed after CSIR's challenge.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: Hoodia (P57) is an appetite suppressant shared with the San people. Turmeric was for wound healing, neem anti-fungal and basmati was RiceTec's patent.

s: Who set up the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (2001)?
x: TKDL was created in 2001 by CSIR and the Ministry of AYUSH.

s: What does TKDL mainly give patent offices to help against biopiracy?
x: TKDL gives patent offices prior-art evidence that the knowledge already exists.

s: With which community did the Hoodia biopiracy case end in a benefit-sharing agreement in 2003?
x: The Hoodia appetite-suppressant case ended in benefit sharing with the San people in 2003.

s: Which one of the following technologies has been flagged for raising concerns about biodiversity?
x: Genetic modification is the technology flagged for biodiversity concerns (APPSC-GS 2023), through gene flow, monoculture and loss of diversity. Drip irrigation, solar panels and rainwater harvesting are not flagged this way.

s: Which of the following is NOT listed as an environmental or health risk of GM crops?
x: Insect resistance, harm to non-target organisms, weediness, genetic homogenisation, toxicity, allergenicity and antibiotic resistance are listed risks; ozone depletion is not a GM-crop risk.

s: Regulation of genetically modified food, including its import, in India rests on which law?
o: Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001
x: GM food is governed by the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, with the FSSAI GM food framework of 2024; import of GM food without approval of the competent authority is prohibited. The EPA governs GMO release, the PPVFR Act plant varieties, and the Patents Act patents.

s: From 1 March 2021, what do imported major food crops into India need?
x: Since 1 March 2021, imported major food crops must carry a 'non-GM cum GM-free' certificate.

s: India's draft GM labelling applies to foods containing what level of GM ingredients?
x: The draft labelling rule covers foods with 1% or more GM ingredient.

s: What did the Biotechnology Regulatory Authority of India (BRAI) Bill, 2013 propose?
o: A ban on all GM crops
A separate patent office for seeds
A GM approval committee in every State
x: The BRAI Bill proposed a single biotechnology regulator but lapsed with the 15th Lok Sabha.

s: Which policy proposes single-window clearance and regulatory sandboxes in the biotechnology sector?
x: The BioE3 Policy, 2024 proposes single-window clearance and regulatory sandboxes.

s: With the end of which Lok Sabha did the BRAI Bill, 2013 lapse?
x: The BRAI Bill proposed a single biotech regulator and lapsed with the 15th Lok Sabha.

s:
Assertion (A): The Cartagena Protocol governs the transboundary movement of living modified organisms.
Reason (R): The Cartagena Protocol entered into force in 2003.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Both are true: the Protocol (adopted 2000, in force 2003) governs transboundary movement of LMOs, but its date of entry into force does not explain its scope.

s: Which country has the largest area under GM crops?
x: The USA leads, followed by Brazil, Argentina, Canada and India; the top five hold over 90% of world GM area.

s: What is India's rank in global GM crop area?
x: India is fifth after the USA, Brazil, Argentina and Canada.

s: Where was the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety adopted in 2000?
x: The Protocol was adopted in 2000 at Montreal and entered into force in 2003.

s: The expression “designer babies” is most directly associated with which ethical debate?
o: Use of adult stem cells for tissue repair
Inspection of laboratories handling moderate-risk agents
Protection of traditional knowledge from patent claims
Use of genetic technologies to select or modify desired human traits
x: “Designer babies” refers to the ethical concern that genetic technologies could be used to select or modify desired traits in human offspring.

s: Lethal agents with no cure, such as Ebola, require which biosafety level?
x: Such agents need BSL-4; BSL-2 is for moderate-risk agents and BSL-3 for serious airborne agents such as TB.

s: The National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017 were issued jointly by which organisations?
x: The National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017 were issued through the ICMR-DBT framework and provide ethical and regulatory guidance.

s: Where and when did He Jiankui carry out the human embryo editing behind the so-called 'CRISPR babies'?
x: He Jiankui’s human embryo-editing experiment in China became widely associated with the “CRISPR babies” controversy in 2018.

s: In which country is Cartagena, after which the Protocol on Biosafety is named?
x: Cartagena is in Colombia; the Protocol is supplementary to the Convention on Biological Diversity.

s: Which Indian law criminalises biological weapons?
x: The WMD Act, 2005 criminalises biological weapons in India; India is also a Party to the BWC (opened 1972, in force 1975).

s: Which of the following is identified as a gap in India’s biosecurity system?
o: Non-membership in the Biological Weapons Convention
Absence of any institution concerned with disease surveillance
Complete prohibition of all genetic engineering research
Absence of a unified national biosecurity framework
x: The stated gap is the absence of a unified national biosecurity framework, with laws also lagging behind synthetic biology and gene editing. India is a party to the BWC.

s: In which year did the Biological Weapons Convention enter into force?
x: The BWC was opened in 1972 and entered into force in 1975; India is a Party.

s: Serious airborne agents such as TB are handled at which biosafety level?
x: BSL-3 is for serious airborne agents like TB; BSL-4 is for lethal agents with no cure like Ebola.

s: The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety is a supplementary agreement to which convention?
x: The Cartagena Protocol is supplementary to the CBD and governs movement of LMOs.

s: Which categories of genome editing did India exempt from its GMO rules in 2022?
x: SDN-1 and SDN-2 add no foreign DNA and are exempt; SDN-3 is regulated as GM.

s: Which genome-editing category is transgenic and remains under full GM regulatory control in India?
x: SDN-3 inserts foreign DNA and stays fully regulated; SDN-1 and SDN-2 make small edits without foreign DNA and are exempt under the 2022 guidelines.

s: Pusa Rice DST1 is associated with which of the following traits and editing features?
o: Insect resistance; insertion of a Bt toxin gene by SDN-2
Drought and salinity tolerance; DST gene knockout by SDN-1
Higher phosphate uptake; insertion of a foreign bacterial gene
Vitamin A enrichment; mitochondrial gene replacement
x: Pusa Rice DST1 is an edited form of MTU1010, designed for drought and salinity tolerance through DST gene knockout using SDN-1.

s: For genome-edited crops covered by the SDN-1 and SDN-2 exemption, which approval route is indicated?
o: IBC approval without the GEAC route
Only approval from the State Pollution Control Board
Approval from the Supreme Court after public consultation
x: Genome-edited crops covered by the SDN-1 and SDN-2 exemption can skip the GEAC route and require IBC approval.

s: Pusa Rice DST1, set for commercial launch as India's first genome-edited rice, was to be regulated like which of the following?
x: Pusa Rice DST1 was described as India’s first genome-edited rice for commercial launch and was to be regulated like a conventional crop.

s: Pusa Rice DST1 was produced by an SDN-1 knockout of which gene?
x: Pusa Rice DST1 is an SDN-1 DST gene knockout in MTU1010, giving drought and salinity tolerance.

s: Which one of the following statements about fullerenes is correct?
o: C60 is a size-tunable semiconductor dot associated with Bawendi and Brus.
C60 is a rolled graphene tube discovered by Sumio Iijima.
C60 is a one-atom-thick sheet associated with Geim and Novoselov.
C60 is known as a buckyball and was associated with Kroto, Curl and Smalley.
x: Fullerene C60 is popularly called a buckyball and is associated with Kroto, Curl and Smalley, who received the Nobel Chemistry Prize in 1996.

s: Graphene is a single atom-thick, sp²-hybridised layer of which form of carbon?
x: Graphene is a one-atom-thick sp² layer of graphite; rolled graphene sheets form carbon nanotubes.

s: What are hollow cylinders of rolled graphene known as?
x: Carbon nanotubes are rolled graphene cylinders; fullerene C60 is a hollow spherical cage of 60 carbon atoms.

s: Which form of carbon is a hollow cage of 60 atoms?
x: Fullerene C60 is the 60-atom cage; graphene is the strong single-atom sheet, graphite the slippery lubricant and diamond the hardest natural substance.

s: How many pentagons and hexagons make up a fullerene C60 molecule?
x: C60, the buckyball, is a cage of 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons.

s: In diamond's tetrahedral network, each carbon atom is bonded to how many other carbon atoms?
x: Each carbon in diamond bonds to four others at the corners of a tetrahedron, giving a rigid 3D network.

s: Graphite is soft and slippery because its layers are held together by which of the following?
x: Graphite's layers are held only by weak van der Waals forces, so they slide over each other.

s: Why is diamond an electrical insulator?
o: Is a hollow cage of 60 atoms
x: Diamond insulates because it has no free electrons; its good heat conduction comes from lattice vibrations, a separate fact.

s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: Fullerene – Semiconductor with a hollow cage structure
Diamond – Transparent, with a very high refractive index
Graphite – Transparent, with a very high refractive index
Activated charcoal – Porous, with a very high surface area
x: Graphite is opaque, black and a good electrical conductor; it is diamond that is transparent and highly refractive.

s: Which material is believed to be harder than diamond?
x: Wurtzite boron nitride is believed harder than diamond.

s: Besides quantum effects, from which property do the unusual properties of nanomaterials mainly arise?
x: Quantum effects and a very high surface-area-to-volume ratio give nanomaterials enhanced reactivity and unusual optical and electrical behaviour.

s: How many metres make one nanometre?
x: 1 nm is one billionth of a metre, 10^-9 m; nanoparticles span 10^-9 to 10^-7 m.

s: Which of the following particle sizes falls within the nanoparticle range?
x: Nanoparticles are 1-100 nm in size, so 50 nm falls in the range.

s: Why do gold nanoparticles look red, purple or blue instead of golden?
o: Because of the surface plasmon effect
Because they lose their gold atoms
Because they are coated with plastic
x: At the nanoscale the surface plasmon effect changes the colour of gold.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Quantum dots — Wound dressing material exclusively
x: Nanoporous materials are used in separation and catalysis. Nanofibres have filtration, smart-clothing and scaffold applications, while nanocrystals are used in LEDs and imaging.

s: Quantum dots are semiconductor nanostructures about how large?
x: Quantum dots are about 1.5-10 nm and show size-set colour.

s: Quantum wells, wires and dots confine electrons in how many dimensions, respectively?
x: Wells confine in 1, wires in 2 and dots in 3 dimensions (2D, 1D and 0D structures).

s: In public health, for what are gold nanoparticles used?
o: Rapid lateral-flow diagnosis of malaria, dengue and typhoid
x: Gold-nanoparticle lateral-flow kits rapidly diagnose malaria, dengue and typhoid; graphene enables bendable wearable sensors.

s: Who developed bendable graphene-based wearable sensors?
x: IISc and C-DAC developed bendable graphene wearable sensors.

s: On which principle does the nanogenerator developed at NCL Pune produce electricity when pressure is applied?
x: The NCL nanogenerator makes electricity from pressure, which is the piezoelectric effect.

s: Which effect lets the quartz crystal in a watch produce an electric charge under mechanical stress?
x: Quartz produces charge under mechanical stress: the piezoelectric effect, also used in nanogenerators.

s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
x: Nano-cellulose is associated with packaging and filters. Heat-based cancer therapy is associated with nano-cups, while silver nanoparticles are used in wound dressings.

s: Which institution developed silver-nanoparticle wound dressings that cut infections by about 60%?
x: CSIR-CGCRI developed silver-nanoparticle wound dressings.

s: With which institute are 'nano-cups' for heat-based cancer therapy associated?
x: INST Mohali developed nano-cups for heat-based cancer therapy and nano-formulations for Parkinson's.

s: For treating which disease were the smart, biodegradable, natural-polymer nanoparticles developed by IIT Mandi designed?
x: IIT Mandi developed renewable-resource-based natural-polymer nanoparticles for colorectal cancer applications.

s: For what is nano-zero-valent iron mainly used in water-related applications?
x: Nano-zero-valent iron is used to remove contaminants from water.

s: Nano-fabrication using which material is used in advanced semiconductor research?
x: Nano-fabrication of silicon is central to advanced semiconductor research and chip making. ITO is for displays and selenium for sensors.

s: The first nano-fabrication facility of Uttarakhand was established by IIT Roorkee. It is intended to complement which missions?
o: National Health Mission, Jal Jeevan Mission and Swachh Bharat Mission
Nano Urea, Nano DAP and Nano-cellulose missions
x: IIT Roorkee’s facility complements the Semiconductor, Nano and Quantum missions; it is not associated with Samudrayaan.

s: Which institute developed a perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell with 27.3% efficiency?
x: IIT Bombay developed a perovskite-silicon tandem cell with 27.3% efficiency.

s: For work on which of the following did Bawendi, Brus and Ekimov receive the 2023 Nobel Prize in Chemistry?
x: The 2023 Chemistry Nobel was for quantum dots, which show size-tunable colour and are used in displays and solar cells.

s: In which year did Binnig and Rohrer, who built the Scanning Tunnelling Microscope in 1981, receive the Nobel Prize in Physics?
x: The STM was made in 1981 and Binnig and Rohrer won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1986.

s: With whom is the classification of nanotechnology products into four generations associated?
x: The four-generation classification of nanoproducts is associated with M. C. Roco.

s: In which year did Kroto, Curl and Smalley receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for fullerene?
x: Fullerene C60 was found in 1985 and the Chemistry Nobel came in 1996.

s: Who received the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics for graphene?
x: Geim and Novoselov of Manchester won the 2010 Physics Nobel for graphene.

s: Who gave the 1959 lecture 'There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom'?
x: Feynman's 1959 lecture is the origin of the idea; Taniguchi coined the term in 1974.

s: Who among the following coined the term 'nanotechnology' in 1974?
x: Norio Taniguchi of Tokyo University coined 'nanotechnology' in 1974; Feynman gave the 1959 lecture.

s: On which surfaces is the Scanning Tunnelling Microscope (STM) used to image atoms?
x: STM images atoms on conducting surfaces, whereas the AFM can work on non-conducting materials as well.

s: Which of the following is a bottom-up method of nanomaterial synthesis?
x: Self-assembly builds structures from atoms and molecules (bottom-up); lithography, milling and etching cut bulk material down (top-down).

s:
Consider the following statements about nanotechnology tools:
1. The STM images only conducting surfaces.
2. The AFM works on non-conductors too.
3. Lithography is a bottom-up method.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The STM needs conductors, while the AFM (1986) also images non-conductors. Lithography is top-down.

s: Lithography, milling and etching are examples of which approach to nanomaterial synthesis?
x: Top-down methods cut bulk material down, such as lithography, milling and etching.

s: Aerosols and nanocoatings belong to which generation of nanoproducts?
x: Passive nanostructures such as aerosols, colloids and coatings form the first generation.

s: Molecular manufacturing is an example of which generation of nanoproducts?
x: The fourth generation, molecular nanosystems, covers molecular manufacturing.

s: What does the third generation of nanoproducts consist of?
x: The third generation is systems of nanosystems, including complex devices such as nanoelectronics and nanomedicine.

s: Which of the following is an engineered, not natural, nanoparticle?
x: Nano-silver is deliberately manufactured; volcanic ash, sea spray and smoke are natural sources of nanoparticles.

s: Under which of the following are dual-use concerns of nanotechnology addressed in India?
x: India has no dedicated nano law; dual-use concerns come under the SCOMET list, while DGFASLI covers occupational risk and FSSAI food.

s: What may nanoparticles cause when they enter cells and organs, leading to nanotoxicity?
x: Nanoparticles may induce oxidative stress and inflammation, with concerns also relating to long-term toxicity, persistence and bioaccumulation.

s: Along with DBT, who issued the Guidelines for Evaluation of Nano-based Agri-input and Food Products (2020)?
x: The 2020 guidelines were brought out by DBT, the Agriculture Ministry and FSSAI.

s: Which of the following concerns has been raised regarding the rapid rollout of nano-urea?
o: The lack of long-term studies before widespread deployment
The complete prohibition of nano-inputs under a nano-specific law
Its inability to be absorbed by plants under any condition
The absence of any possible agricultural use
x: A major criticism is that nano-urea has been rolled out rapidly without adequate long-term studies. The concern is about evidence and safety assessment, not the complete absence of agricultural use.

s: What is the indicated nitrogen-use efficiency of Nano Urea?
x: Nano Urea has an indicated nitrogen-use efficiency of about 70%, against about 30–35% for conventional urea.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Nano Urea?
o: Its particle size is about 20–50 nm
It is applied as a foliar spray
It may reduce urea use by up to about 25%
x: Nano Urea does not fully replace conventional urea; it is a 20–50 nm foliar spray that may cut urea use by up to about 25%.

s: In which year was the specification of Nano DAP notified under the Fertiliser Control Order?
x: Nano DAP was notified under the FCO on 2 March 2023; it is used for seed treatment and foliar application.

s: What is the particle size of IFFCO's liquid Nano Urea?
x: Nano Urea is a liquid with 20-50 nm particles used as a foliar spray.

s: What is Nano DAP meant for?
x: Nano DAP, notified on 2 March 2023, is used for seed treatment and foliar spray.

s: Under which department was the Nano Mission launched in 2007 as an umbrella programme?
x: The Nano Mission (2007) is a DST umbrella programme, with an initial outlay of about Rs 1,000 crore for five years.

s: What was the outlay of the Nano Mission approved in 2007?
x: The Nano Mission (DST) was approved on 3 May 2007 with Rs 1,000 crore for five years.

s: In which year was Phase II of the Nano Mission, with Rs 650 crore, approved?
x: Phase II was approved in 2014 for the 12th Plan with Rs 650 crore.

s: In which year was the National Quantum Mission approved?
x: The National Quantum Mission was approved on 19 April 2023 with Rs 6,003.65 crore.

s: What is the outlay of the National Quantum Mission (2023-24 to 2030-31)?
x: The National Quantum Mission, approved on 19 April 2023, has an outlay of Rs 6,003.65 crore.
